claims.text: Increasing Hf relative to Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr in HfNbTaTiZr increases lattice distortion.
The increased lattice distortion provides greater solid-solution strengthening and raises yield strength and hardness.
Increasing Hf content may reduce ductility.
The baseline is an equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy prepared from elemental powders.
The starting elemental powders are high-purity and initially mixed without intentional composition modification.
Composition can be varied by increasing Hf by 5–10 at.% and reducing one or more other constituent elements.
The basic BCC phase can remain intact under the proposed 5–10 at.% Hf enrichment.
High-energy mechanical alloying followed by spark plasma sintering is a usable processing route for HfNbTaTiZr.
Holding SPS temperature, pressure, and time constant minimizes processing-related variation between composition groups.
Composition-induced changes in atomic-size mismatch cause lattice distortion and may alter phase distribution.
Changing composition may produce minor secondary phases or interstitial oxides.
Hf is a larger-atomic-radius constituent whose enrichment increases local lattice strain.
Lattice distortion impedes dislocation motion.
Oxide or carbide secondary phases may create stress-concentration sites and reduce ductility.
Hf-enriched alloys will have approximately 10–15% higher yield strength and hardness than the equiatomic baseline.
Hf-enriched alloys may have approximately 10–20% lower ductility than the equiatomic baseline.
The proposed effects apply within individual-element composition changes of approximately ±5–10 at.%, whereas larger deviations may cause phase separation or brittle secondary phases.
XRD and SEM can be used to characterize phases and microstructure in processed HfNbTaTiZr specimens.
Vickers hardness testing can quantify hardness in processed HfNbTaTiZr specimens.
Tensile or compression testing can determine yield strength and ductility for the proposed composition series.

contradictions.description: The ductility reduction is presented as tentative ('may' or 'might') and explicitly uncertain, but the falsification rule treats failure to observe a ductility decrease as sufficient to falsify the full hypothesis.
